```{r}
  th
```

Forest fires in Canada released `r format(round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / 1000), big.mark = ",")` Mt of carbon dioxide in 2023 on the FAOSTAT Tier 1 estimate, `r round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / mean(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year < 2023]), 1)` times the mean of the earlier years and `r round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2020], 0)` times the quietest year, 2020, at `r format(round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2020] / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1)` Mt (@fig-canada-forest).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-source-gap
#| tbl-cap: "Carbon dioxide from fires in other forest in Canada, as FAOSTAT computes it at Tier 1 and as Canada reported it to the UNFCCC, for the years both are available. FAOSTAT carries the reported series inside the same domain."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(gap, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-source-gap.csv")
fmt_tbl(gap)
```

Across the `r nrow(gap)` years both sources reported, the FAOSTAT Tier 1 estimate was a median of `r round(median(gap$Ratio), 1)` times the value Canada submitted, from `r min(gap$Ratio)` times in `r gap$Year[which.min(gap$Ratio)]` to `r max(gap$Ratio)` times in `r gap$Year[which.max(gap$Ratio)]` (@tbl-source-gap).

## FAOSTAT's coefficients

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefficients
#| tbl-cap: "Fuel consumption and emission factors FAOSTAT applied to fires in Canada, 2001 to 2024, recovered from its own published values by dividing the biomass burned of each item by its burned area and each emission by the biomass burned, with the rows of Tables 2.4 and 2.5 of the 2006 IPCC Guidelines that the values equal. Carbon dioxide is not reported for the savanna, grassland and shrubland items."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(coefficients, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-coefficients.csv")
fmt_tbl(coefficients)
```

FAOSTAT's published values for Canada showed which coefficients it had applied (@tbl-coefficients). Its biomass burned divided by its burned area gave `r sprintf("%.1f", min(used$fuel[used$item == "Other forest"]))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(used$fuel[used$item == "Other forest"]))` tonnes of dry matter per hectare for other forest. That range lay between the 41.0 of Table 2.4 for all boreal forest and the 50.4 for all other temperate forests, as allocation by ecological zone would give [@aalde2006generic; @fao2025fires]. Its emissions divided by its biomass burned gave `r coefficients[["CO2 (g/kg)"]][coefficients$Item == "Other forest"]` g of carbon dioxide, `r coefficients[["CH4 (g/kg)"]][coefficients$Item == "Other forest"]` g of methane and `r coefficients[["N2O (g/kg)"]][coefficients$Item == "Other forest"]` g of nitrous oxide per kilogram of dry matter burned in forest fires in every year. These were the factors of Table 2.5 for savanna and grassland rather than those for extra tropical forest, `r format(table_2_5$co2[2], big.mark = ",")`, `r table_2_5$ch4[2]` and `r table_2_5$n2o[2]`, a row the table notes "includes all other forest types" [@aalde2006generic]. The methane FAOSTAT reported for Canada's forest fires was therefore `r round(100 * table_2_5$ch4[1] / table_2_5$ch4[2])` per cent of what its cited factors gave, the nitrous oxide `r round(100 * table_2_5$n2o[1] / table_2_5$n2o[2])` per cent and the carbon dioxide `r round(100 * table_2_5$co2[1] / table_2_5$co2[2])` per cent. The domain also placed `r round(100 * sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]]) / sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]] + savanna_share[["Forest fires"]]))` per cent of the area it recorded as burned in Canada over 2001 to 2024, and `r round(savanna_share$share[savanna_share$year == 2023])` per cent in 2023, in its savanna, grassland and shrubland items. To these it applied the Table 2.4 values for savanna woodland and grassland burned in the mid or late dry season, `r table_2_4$fuel[3]` and `r table_2_4$fuel[4]` tonnes per hectare, and it reported no carbon dioxide for them.

## Classifying a fire year as natural

```{r}
#| label: tbl-baselines
#| tbl-cap: "The natural disturbance threshold applied to Canadian forest fire emissions under three baseline lengths. The threshold is the baseline mean plus two standard deviations, and the years listed are those the rule classifies as natural."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(baselines, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-baselines.csv")
fmt_tbl(baselines)
```

The baseline length moved the threshold but not the classification. Lengthening the baseline from 13 to 20 years raised the threshold from `r format(baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1], big.mark = ",")` to `r format(baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2], big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide, a rise of `r round(100 * (baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2] / baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1] - 1))` per cent, and both lengths classed the same `r length(strsplit(baselines[["Years classified natural"]][1], ", ")[[1]])` years as natural, `r baselines[["Years classified natural"]][1]` (@tbl-baselines). A 30 year baseline could not be run, because the FAOSTAT series covered only `r nrow(forest_co2)` years derived from observations, 2001 to 2024, and the earlier years were filled rather than measured.

## Crediting with and without the separation

```{r}
#| label: tbl-credits
#| tbl-cap: "Emissions and reductions for Canada's managed land under the two accounts, 2017 to 2024, on a 2012 to 2016 reference period. The disaggregated account is the human activity component Canada reports; the undisaggregated account is the sum of the human activity and natural disturbance components. A negative reduction is emissions above the crediting level, which the standard treats as a reversal."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(credits, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-credits.csv")
fmt_tbl(credits)
```


The separation decided whether there was anything to credit. On the account Canada reported, reductions were positive in `r sum(split_pos)` of the `r nrow(credits)` crediting years and summed to `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent, with `r sum(!split_pos)` years below the crediting level, `r credits$Year[!split_pos][1]` at `r credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][!split_pos][1]` Mt and `r credits$Year[!split_pos][2]` at `r credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][!split_pos][2]` Mt. Without the separation, reductions were positive in only `r sum(whole_pos)` years, and the shortfall in `r credits$Year[worst]` alone reached `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt, `r round(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]) / sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]))` times every reduction the disaggregated account achieved over the period (@tbl-credits).

Neither deduction applied in that case, because there was nothing to deduct from. The standard's reversal rule retired buffer credits equal to the lower of the emissions above the crediting level or every credit issued, so an undisaggregated account of this land exhausted its buffer in `r credits$Year[which(!whole_pos)[1]]` and again in each later year that emissions exceeded the level [@art2021trees].

## Crediting in British Columbia

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bc
#| tbl-cap: "Emissions and reductions for British Columbia under the two accounts, 2017 to 2024, on a 2012 to 2016 reference period. Both components are the provincial figures of the national inventory, and the burned area share is the province's share of the area burned in Canada."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(bc_credits, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-bc.csv")
fmt_tbl(bc_credits)
```


British Columbia followed the national pattern more sharply. The province had `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2018]` per cent of the area burned in Canada in 2018 and `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2023]` per cent in 2023. On the disaggregated account its reductions were positive in `r sum(bc_split_pos)` of the `r nrow(bc_credits)` crediting years, summing to `r round(sum(bc_credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent, and without the separation they were positive in `r sum(bc_whole_pos)` years, with `r bc_credits$Year[bc_worst]` falling `r format(abs(bc_credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt below the crediting level (@tbl-bc).

## The uncertainty of each account

```{r}
#| label: tbl-uncertainty
#| tbl-cap: "Reductions and their uncertainty for Canada under the two accounts, from 10,000 Monte Carlo draws using the annual flux uncertainty published for Canada's forest carbon model. The interval is the 90 per cent interval the standard requires, its half width expressed against the mean reduction of the same draws, and the deduction is what the standard's adjustment factor takes from it. A percentage is printed only where the mean reduction is positive, since a percentage of a shortfall carries no meaning, and the undisaggregated deduction is therefore not reported."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(uncertainty, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-uncertainty.csv")
fmt_tbl(uncertainty)
```

Canada's own uncertainty analysis of its model reported a 95 per cent interval `r round(32.2 * 44 / 12)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent wide around a median of `r round(-0.8 * 44 / 12, 1)` Mt, and stated that this interval "cannot be meaningfully expressed in percentage terms because its range of possible values contains zero" [@metsaranta2017uncertainty]. In the crediting arithmetic the interval was wider than the reductions it qualified. Across the `r sum(!is.na(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]]))` crediting years with a positive mean reduction, the interval of the disaggregated account ran from `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent of its mean reduction, and the implied uncertainty deduction from `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent (@tbl-uncertainty). The separation restored the sign of the account but left the credit uncertain by more than its own size.

## What survives the deductions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kept
#| tbl-cap: "The share of gross reductions and removals a jurisdiction keeps under the standard, by the reported uncertainty. The uncertainty deduction follows Equation 11 and the buffer follows Table 2 of the standard. The last column is the worst case in the five years after a reversal, when the buffer rises by five percentage points."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(deductions, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-kept.csv")
fmt_tbl(deductions)
```


The two deductions were linear in the reported uncertainty, so the uncertainty at which a jurisdiction kept nothing could be solved directly. On the default buffer it was `r round(100 * break_even())` per cent, with all three mitigating factors and the smallest buffer `r round(100 * break_even("1,2,3"))` per cent, and in the five years after a reversal `r round(100 * break_even(after_reversal = TRUE))` per cent. At an uncertainty of 100 per cent a jurisdiction kept `r deductions[["Kept, 25% buffer (%)"]][deductions[[1]] == 100]` per cent of its gross reductions and removals on the default buffer, and at 150 per cent it kept `r deductions[["Kept, 25% buffer (%)"]][deductions[[1]] == 150]` per cent (@tbl-kept). Uncertainty of that size was not hypothetical, since the worked example of the uncertainty chapter printed ±150 per cent for one land category [@paciornik2019uncertainties].

## Fires in organic soils

```{r}
#| label: tbl-canada-peat
#| tbl-cap: "Burned area and emissions from fires in organic soils in Canada, as FAO computed them and then set them to zero in the published Emissions from Fires domain. Values for 1990 to 1995 are the average of the reconstructed series rather than observations, which is why they do not vary."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(canada, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-canada-peat.csv")
fmt_tbl(canada)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-canada-peat
#| fig-cap: "Burned area of fires in organic soils in Canada, 1990 to 2021, from the FAO table that the published domain replaces with zeros. The flat section to 1995 is the filled part of the series and the rest is derived from satellite observations."
#| echo: true

ggplot2::ggplot(canada, ggplot2::aes(Year, `Burned area (ha)` / 1000)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Burned area (thousand ha)") +
  th
```


Over the `r nrow(obs)` years of the satellite record, 2001 to 2021, fires in organic soils in Canada burned a mean of `r format(round(mean(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares a year. They released `r format(round(mean(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide and `r format(round(mean(obs[["CH4 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of methane a year, none of which appeared in the FAOSTAT domain a government downloaded. The largest year was `r obs$Year[which.max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]`, at `r format(round(max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares and `r format(round(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]][which.max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide, and the smallest was `r obs$Year[which.min(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]`, at `r format(round(min(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares.

The six years from 1990 to 1995 repeated one value, `r format(round(fill), big.mark = ",")` hectares, which was the mean of every later year to the last digit the table printed, `r format(round(mean(post[["Burned area (ha)"]]), 2), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 2)` hectares for 1996 to 2021 against `r format(round(fill, 2), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 2)`. The filled years were therefore the average of the whole remaining series rather than of the window the methodological note described, so any mean over the full series returned that value whatever the observations did.

# Discussion

On the components of Canada's 2026 inventory, separating natural disturbance decided whether an account existed to credit in 2017 to 2024, but it did not make that account precise. The managed land of the country reported reductions in `r sum(split_pos)` of the `r nrow(credits)` years, totalling `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent, while the same land without the separation reported them in `r sum(whole_pos)` years and fell `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt short of its crediting level in 2023 alone. British Columbia, with `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2023]` per cent of the area burned in Canada that year, reversed in the same way, reporting `r round(sum(bc_credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_split_pos]), 1)` Mt separated against a shortfall of `r format(abs(bc_credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt. The separation was therefore the condition on which a jurisdictional credit existed rather than an adjustment to a reported number. Earlier work found the same dependence in reporting, where natural disturbance was among the reasons Canada did not elect forest management under the Kyoto Protocol [@kurz2008risk] and a revised harvest record moved the reported human sink by 113 Mt CO~2~e in 1990 [@kurz2024revised]. The treatment of wildfire as natural also separated a forestry source of 90.8 Mt CO~2~e a year from a reported sink of 4.7 Mt [@bysouth2024high]. In each case the partition rather than the forest moved the balance, and a standard that took the reported balance as its input passed the partition straight into the credit.

The rest of this Discussion took in turn the uncertainty of a net near zero, the record and regrowth period behind the separation and the fire emission method, then the buffers of the standards and the changes that would close these gaps.

The separated account kept part of its reductions in only `r sum(banked > 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(banked))` years with a positive reduction, for an arithmetic rather than an ecological reason. An account whose emissions and removals nearly cancelled reported a percentage uncertainty far larger than either side of it, the case @paciornik2019uncertainties warned against interpreting. Canada's own inventory met the same limit in 2024, printing the 95 per cent interval of the carbon dioxide of Forest Land, a net of −1.9 Mt within −63 to 19 Mt, as 3,100 and −1,100 per cent [@eccc2026nir]. Applied to the crediting equations, the published interval gave uncertainty deductions of `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent, larger than the reduction in `r sum(over, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(over))` years with a positive reduction and smaller only in `r paste(uncertainty$Year[which(!over)], collapse = " and ")`. The separation thus moved the reported quantity away from zero in the years the fires dominated and left it near zero in the others. In `r mc_split$Year[which(banked > 0)]` the account kept `r round(banked[which(banked > 0)], 1)` per cent of its reduction, after the uncertainty deduction and a buffer that the shortfall of `r min(credits$Year[!split_pos])` had raised to `r 100 * trees_buffer(after_reversal = TRUE)` per cent. Regional budgets elsewhere were also near zero within their uncertainty, and in California the data could not establish whether the land was a source or a sink [@haverd2013australian; @rosan2023contemporary; @divittorio2021quantifying]. The standards differed in what such an interval cost. The adjustment factor of ART TREES rose with the interval without limit [@art2021trees], whereas the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility capped its uncertainty set-aside at 15 per cent [@fcpf2024buffer], under which a positive reduction kept at least `r round(100 * (1 - 0.15) * (1 - 0.40))` per cent of itself after both set-asides.

The length of the record mattered less to the classification than to the threshold. Lengthening the baseline from 13 to 20 years raised the threshold by `r round(100 * (baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2] / baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1] - 1))` per cent and marked the same five years, and a 30 year baseline could not be tested because the satellite record covered only `r nrow(forest_co2)` years. The fire regime literature found estimates sensitive to the record in the same way, with Weibull parameters that changed between 22 and 31 years of data [@oliveira2011fire] and fire cycle estimates degraded by short-term variation in fire activity [@cyr2016quantifying]. Fire cycles in Canada ran from 50 to 769 years [@johnson1991climatically; @arsenault2016unravelling], so a baseline of 13 to 30 years sampled a small part of one cycle. Fire history therefore turned to centuries of tree rings and millennia of charcoal wherever recent fires were too few [@gavin2007forest]. Of the three crediting documents read for this study, only Verra's tool set a record length, 100 years with no fewer than 20 [@verra2024nprt]. Canada applied no baseline at all, reconstructing instead the cause of every stand for 1889 to 1989 and keeping each burned area in the natural category for the 60 to 100 years it took to regrow to a harvestable age [@kurz2024revised]. Australia tested fire seasons against a 13 year mean [@bowman2023wildfire], and the European example in the guidance used the 20 years before the base year and assumed 20 years of regrowth [@ogle2019generic]. Three implementations thus used three temporal designs under guidance that specified none. The regrowth half of the account also contained the error of the model, which underestimated the net biomass gain of undisturbed boreal stands by 10 per cent over 71 years [@bernier2010reconstructing]. That regrowth was what returned to the human account when a burned stand crossed the age threshold.

The fire emissions inside both accounts came from one method. Canada's fire matrices assumed high severity throughout, and a severity-based sub-model gave regional emissions typically 10 to 25 per cent lower [@thompson2026incorporating]. Both accounts shared that difference, and the account without the separation took nearly all of it, because Canada placed every wildfire in the natural component [@eccc2026nir]. FAOSTAT's Tier 1 estimate ran a median of `r round(median(gap$Ratio), 1)` times the value Canada submitted, which put the choice of source on the same scale as the choice of method. Part of that gap lay in coefficients the methodological note did not state. FAOSTAT applied the savanna and grassland emission factors to Canada's forest fires, which put its methane at `r round(100 * table_2_5$ch4[1] / table_2_5$ch4[2])` per cent of what its cited method gave. It also placed `r round(100 * sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]]) / sum(savanna_share[["Savanna fires"]] + savanna_share[["Forest fires"]]))` per cent of the area it recorded as burned in savanna, grassland and shrubland items, which it burned at the fuel values of tropical savanna and reported without carbon dioxide. Most of the area FAOSTAT recorded as burned in Canada therefore contributed no carbon dioxide to the estimate a government would check its inventory against. Differences of this size were common among fire estimates [@kukavskaya2013fire; @vallet2025soil], and FAOSTAT's estimate of the global land sector differed in sign from what countries reported [@grassi2022carbon]. The same database set Canada's organic soil fire emissions to zero while computing them at a mean of `r format(round(mean(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide a year over the satellite record [@fao2025fires].

The buffers withheld against reversal did not follow the fire regime of the land they covered. ART TREES applied 25 per cent to every jurisdiction unless three mitigating factors were met [@art2021trees], and the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility added 0 to 5 percentage points for exposure to natural disturbance [@fcpf2024buffer]. Only Verra's tool scored the history of events in the area itself, and then for projects rather than jurisdictions [@verra2024nprt]. Fire cycles in Canada differed more than tenfold between regions [@johnson1991climatically; @belisle2011fire; @arsenault2016unravelling], and North American conifer forests were among those with the highest reversal risk [@wu2026global]. British Columbia, with `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2018]` per cent of the area burned in Canada in 2018 and `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2023]` per cent in 2023, fell `r format(abs(bc_credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt short on its own unseparated account. These were grounds for buffer contributions set from regional fire regime statistics, as the contributions prepared for the carbon removals regulation of the European Union were set from modelled regional loss to disturbance [@marinelli2026risk].

Crediting standards inherited the silence of the guidance, because the REDD+ Environmental Excellence Standard allowed natural disturbance to be excluded on the authority of the guidance without saying how far back the record must reach [@art2025trees3; @ogle2019generic]. Two jurisdictions applying the same clause to the same fire record could therefore report different natural shares, depending on how far back their labelling reached and how long their regrowth ran. Four changes would close the gap, the first being to specify the record length behind any natural disturbance test and the second to state the regrowth period over which later removals were disaggregated. The third was to take the uncertainty deduction from gross emissions and gross removals rather than from a net near zero, and the fourth to set buffer contributions from the regional fire regime.

Two limits qualified these results, the first being that the uncertainty analysis applied one published interval to every annual flux, which assumed the model was as certain of a quiet year as of a megafire year. The second was that both accounts used Canada's figures as reported, so the study compared two sums of one model's output, with fire matrices that assumed high severity [@thompson2026incorporating], and FAOSTAT was its only independent estimate.

# Conclusions

Run through the crediting level, uncertainty deduction and buffer of the REDD+ Environmental Excellence Standard for 2017 to 2024, Canada's managed land achieved `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent with natural disturbance separated and fell `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt short in 2023 alone without it. A jurisdiction in a megafire regime could therefore report a creditable balance only by excluding the fires, under guidance that set no record length for doing so. The separated account remained uncertain by more than its own size, with uncertainty deductions of `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent, and kept part of its reductions only in `r mc_split$Year[which(banked > 0)]`, `r round(banked[which(banked > 0)], 1)` per cent of them. FAOSTAT's fire estimate for Canada, the independent check a government reached for, rested on savanna emission factors and savanna fuel values that its method did not state. Standards that relied on the separation needed a stated record length, a stated regrowth period, an uncertainty deduction on gross fluxes and buffers set from regional fire regimes. The code and data behind every number here were published so that a government could repeat the comparison.
